Monday Bittensor Series Week 24 - Centralised Vs Decentralised AI

On Tuesday 9th June 2026, Anthropic released to the public its most advanced AI model to date, Fable 5 — a modified version of its internal “Mythos” model, which it had previously deemed unsafe to release publicly due to cybersecurity concerns. While Fable 5 was designed with safeguards in place, three days later the US Government issued export controls barring foreign nationals from using the technology. Anthropic was reportedly given 90 minutes to comply and has since taken its most advanced models offline for all users.

This move by the US Government highlights a core problem with AI developed by centralised entities: it is beholden to the governments whose jurisdictions they sit within. Last year we saw this with DeepSeek, where Chinese censorship laws prohibited certain information from being disclosed by its AI model, such as the events of Tiananmen Square in 1989. Now the US, known for its embrace of pioneering innovation, is placing restrictions on and interfering with the technology.

When searching Google, we don’t always get the most relevant results at the top of the page, and it is often dominated by paid advertisements and priority listings. The latest AI models from big corporations are said to be adopting a similar strategy, bringing into question the truth and relevance of their responses.

If centralised AI companies are allowing their models to respond according to paid partnerships and governments are restricting content and models, what is the alternative?

Bittensor $TAO

Co-founders Jacob Steeves and Ala Shaabana foresaw these issues, developing Bittensor as an open-source, decentralised AI and machine-learning network that has since become the largest in the world by market cap and overall network activity.

Developed in the same spirit as Bitcoin, which has given power back to the people as an antidote to currency debasement, Bittensor is giving power back to the people with AI — beholden to no single entity or government. No one is excluded from participating, your data is not secretly used for training, and those building on the network are incentivised to compete and collaborate in a transparent, permissionless environment.

In the same way Bitcoin cannot be shut down, Bittensor’s top builders (subnets) are becoming similarly indispensable. Chutes, Subnet 64, comprises a global network of miners who provide inference power for open-source AI models. Iota, Subnet 9, represents a global pool of miners training open-source AI models. These are just two examples of 128 decentralised builders.

If you’re new to or unfamiliar with decentralised AI and Bittensor, a good entry product to experiment with is called BlueTAO: https://t.co/EWwVWeUTa1 

BlueTAO acts as a “frontend” to Bittensor, using a modified, private version of a latest DeepSeek open-source AI model hosted on Chutes, Subnet 64. Search prompts are handled by Desearch, Subnet 22, and there is also an AI image detector powered by BitMind, Subnet 34, where users can check if an image is AI-generated or real.

In the few days after Anthropic was served a US Government directive to shut off its latest AI models, Bittensor’s price rose 36%. 

Coincidence or not, the timing is certainly telling.

Check back next Monday for more on Bittensor $TAO

Anthropic built a model so powerful they gave it to the government before the public ever saw it.

Then they added safeguards. Then they released it anyway.

It's called Claude Fable 5. Mythos class. The same tier that Anthropic internally flagged as too capable for an open release — until they decided the world was ready.

Here's what's already happening with it:

→ A developer rebuilt Mario Kart 64 from scratch using 2 sentences as the entire prompt 
→ Stripe gave it an engineering task that their team had scoped at several months of work — Fable 5 closed it in 1 day 
→ I prompted it once with a vague business description and it returned a fully functional 3D website — layout, animations, copy, structure

The benchmarks aren't even close. Every major eval that other frontier models compete on, Fable 5 is sitting above them.

To access it right now — open Claude, click the model selector in the top left, and you'll see Fable 5 listed. No waitlist. No application. It's already there.

One thing worth knowing before you go all in: this model is expensive on tokens. It's not the right tool for simple tasks, summaries, or quick rewrites. The older Claude models handle that better and cheaper.

Fable 5 is for the heavy lifts. Complex codebases. Multi-system architectures. Problems that have been sitting on your list because no model felt capable enough to actually solve them.

That's where it's genuinely different. Not in the marketing — in the output.

The gap between what this model can build and what most people think AI is capable of right now is still enormous. The people closing that gap first are going to have a serious advantage for the next 12 months.

I didn't finish my testing, but expect that Fable 5 would score somewhere around GPT-5.4 (xhigh) on my benchmark.  This is based on early testing, not a fully baked conclusion.

The model's legal research capabilities are up there with GPT-5.4 (xhigh), maybe even GPT-5.5 (xhigh).  Its needle-in-the-haystack search capabilities are very poor.  There were a few cases where it found the correct website where the answer to the question would be found, but still failed to fish out the correct info.

No comparison to GPT-5.5 Pro.

The U.S. government’s action against Anthropic’s Fable 5 and Mythos 5 does not mean AI is ending. Instead, it shows that AI has reached a more serious stage.

Frontier AI is no longer seen as just software; it is now tied to national security, global competition, regulation, and technological power.

Anthropic said the government’s rules about foreign-national access made them turn off these models for everyone, which highlights how sensitive and important advanced AI has become.

Still, we should not only react with fear. Every major technology has faced problems: electricity brought safety risks, aviation had crashes, the internet led to cybercrime and misinformation, social media changed politics and culture, and biotech raised tough ethical questions.

None of these technologies disappeared. They improved, became safer, were regulated, and became part of daily life.

AI will go through the same process. There will be mistakes, limits, political pressure, and real risks, but once people see what technology can do, it cannot be stopped. You can slow it down, regulate it, and ask for better safeguards, but you cannot undo progress.

The positive side is that moments like this can help the AI industry grow up, with better safety, governance, transparency, and more responsible creators.

AI will have problems, just like other powerful technologies, but the future will not be shaped by fear. It will be shaped by people who understand the risks, fix the problems, and keep moving humanity forward.

This is not the end of AI.
This is AI maturing.
